newsitem.title: USA: U.S. opposes boycott of Serbia elections.
newsitem.headline: U.S. opposes boycott of Serbia elections.

text.p: The United States said on Tuesday it opposes a boycott of Serbian elections by opposition parties even though poll conditions are "grossly unfair" and Yugoslav President Slobodan Milosevic has refused to make changes.

State Department spokesman James Rubin acknowledged that "electoral conditions in Serbia at this time are neither fully free or fair" because opposition parties are denied equal access to the media and voting districts have been configured to favour the ruling Socialist Party.

Also, the fact that the government has refused to allow international monitors unfettered access to the country "suggests that Belgrade has something to hide" in advance of the Sept. 21 presidential and parliamentary elections, he told reporters.
Nevertheless, Rubin refused to endorse a boycott of the process declared by some opposition groups saying "boycotts are not particularly effective tools for bringing about political change."
"It wouldn't be right for the United States to advise Serbian opposition parties on an election boycott. That is a choice that the individual political parties must make themselves," he said.
"In general, however, the United States favours the broadest participation in the political process," he added.

The spokesman articulated a more diplomatic and understanding view than special U.S. envoy Richard Holbrooke, who said in the Balkans last weekend: "... parties that boycott the elections (don't) do anything anything but damage themselves. It's stupid to boycott the elections."
U.S. sources said opposition parties were "dispirited" by the message.

Rubin stressed that "we recognise that the decision whether or not to participate in the upcoming Serbian presidential and parliamentary elections under grossly unfair electoral conditions is a difficult one."

"So we are not telling them (opposition parties) that their failure to participate will somehow affect our view of them. We're not pulling out all the stops" to encourage opposition groups to take part in the polls, he said.

On their mission last weekend, Holbrooke and U.S. permanent envoy on Bosnia Robert Gelbard told Milosevic that "over the long term, the support that the international community has for him will be determined by the democratic conditions in Serbia," Rubin said.
But "it doesn't appear that he's (Milosevic) going to make fundamental changes," the spokesman added.
